blocks.x: Okay, we're going? We're going. Just so that the secretaries will know what's what,
can you give me your right name? My correct name is Edward Timothy Kelly. Okay. I'm popularly known as Tim. And what are you unpopular? The old man. No, him. Oh. What are you called? John.
What is your whole name? John Griffin Jones. Okay. So, and he's, well, where are we?
This is the building of the Department of Archives and History in Jackson. This is a meeting room. Mm-hmm. Where they show films and have symposium meetings and that sort of thing.

Yeah. So, really what we're trying to do today is to break him in and talk, how to do an interview and about music and we're going to talk about music in Mississippi among other things. Oh, that's great. Even though I'm doing it for Tulane, I think it would be nice for Johnny to hear how we operate. Operate the opportunity. No, not at all. I didn't put down my name, too. My name is Dick Allen. My right name is Richard Binion Allen, but I don't like to give the whole thing too often. It's not a very euphonious name. I get kidded about it a lot. Anyhow, uh, what I do is I ask Tim a question and then the tape runs out. That's about it. Tim is very easy to talk to and he's, I think, given us a wonderful interview before. And I want to clear up a few things like dates and your sister's names and so forth. Uh, because it is hard to unscramble a person's life and I try to think of landmarks from that period. Like, uh, who were you playing with when World War I started?
Well, that's a little early for me. I was, uh, I was working on the, uh, war bond drive with the Boy Scouts. Really? Helping raise money for Uncle Sam.
I see.
By going around and we would appear in theaters and other public places and make a pitch for, uh, Liberty Barnes. Uh-huh. And that's what I was playing.
And, uh, World War I. Did, were you actually playing an instrument then?
The beginning of World War I I would have been, uh, about 12 or so, just before I had taken up the clarinet.
I see. Were your sisters playing music then?

Uh, both of my sisters, uh, one of them, Mrs. Mary G. Kelly of Alexandria, Louisiana. The other, Mrs. Nanny B. Elkins of Kerrville, Texas, both studied pianos for about eight years. Both played very well. But at the time, girls were supposed to study piano. They all did. Yeah. And, uh, we did have a nice upright piano and I lived in, thank goodness.
That's G as in George and B as in Baker.
That's right.
I'm trying to get those two middle initials in order correctly. And it's nice to have every detail right if you can. And, uh, so then what happened, say, do you remember November the 11th of 1918?
Well, I remember the happy day of Armistice Day. I remember it very well.
Mm-hmm.

I had lived in Marshall, Texas at that time. And, uh, Marshall was a very good little town. We had a college of Marshall, which was a Baptist college. And, uh, they had gone into the ROTC business pretty substantially. So, uh, all of the young people who would not have to go to war were extremely happy about that. Sure, I remember it well.
Were you still in school then? Oh, yeah. Did they have a celebration? Were people bringing out, breaking out horns?

Well, as well as I remember, they had, uh, parades downtown celebrating the end of the war. And, uh, I don't remember specifically what, but, uh, all over America they celebrated. Mm-hmm. The end of it had been a terrible war. Oh, yeah.
And, uh, well, we talked about your, the way you finished school, and, uh, several times, maybe, I don't remember. But, uh, what age were you when you first went off to play in a band?

Dick, I left Marshall about 1922. I, uh, my last half year in high school. I really didn't finish high school. And, uh, I went out with the Ham Crawford band, which we talked about before. And, uh, then I really never returned, except just to see my folks occasionally. But then on, I've been out in various capacities as a music man, or clarinetist, or saxophonist, or whatever.

I think I didn't ask you something I wanted to about Ham Crawford. I believe it was Wingy, and I, this has been several months back, uh, since I even read the book. But he mentioned Wenslow, Arizona, Ham being out there.

Um, Ham played all out through the West. And when he was with him for a time, when he was also out there with Doc Ross for a time, we talked about that. But, uh, Ham Crawford, uh, organized little bands and took them everywhere. And somehow he would just end up, he'd come into a town and pick all the best musicians and offer them wonderful, a wonderful future. And sometimes it materialized, sometimes it didn't. But at least he always was able to attract the best of the young musicians, because they're always ready to leave home, you know. Just a chance to play, that's the thing. Oh, sure.
And, uh, did he, did you and Wingy work with him at the same time? No.

No. I didn't meet Wingy until several years later. Uh-huh. And, uh, I met him in Shreveport. And I had first heard of Wingy when I was playing with the Budysburg Mountain Boys. And I remember a little drug store over in Meridian where we looked at a picture of a wild New Orleans band, all posed and everything. And of course we were attracted to it and so we asked who they were and we called them the Crescent City Jazzers or something like that, from Mobile.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, Wingy was the trumpet player. I remember the other people, but that's my first, uh, knowledge of Wingy. And then, of course, historically I've known Wingy closely and well over a period of, uh, more than 50 years.
I think almost all those Crescent City Jazzers ago. Jeff Riddick's brother, Johnny, played with him at one time.
That's right. And I knew Johnny. He was a band harmonica player, if I'm not mistaken, also. Really?
Hmm.

And, uh, and one of the Riddicks, of course I knew Jeff through his affiliation with Wildlands and the Warriors, and I knew him more so as a player. Yeah. He's, he's a good, well-routined New Orleans piano player.
Did you know Avery Loposa from Mobile?
This, I think he probably was in this group.
Oh.
But I did not know him.
I don't like to put words in your mouth or anything. You know, I just could think of some of the guys in that band. All right.
Well, I.

Felix Carino. Mm-hmm. Well, and, uh, I think all of them are gone except one, and I can't remember which one was there, somebody. Like Jeff, I think, was telling me about it. And, uh, you can't get around to meet everybody. It took me long enough to meet you.
Ha ha. Well, I'm certainly glad we finally got together. Oh, yeah.
Well, uh, I didn't get about the different Irish musicians in your family down, but, uh, quite pat. I don't know how many of them there were.

Uh, actually, I don't have much background as far as, uh, relatives, or ancestors who played music. Uh, the Irish part of my family were people who, uh, were kind of in the theater and, uh, interested in the arts. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Well educated, but no musical background. I told you of my great uncle Gus Clayton, who was a country peddler and a very good one. And that's about as much of a background as far as having inherited any talent or anything long as mine.
You don't remember the Irish people in the family singing any songs from the old country in particular, right?

No, we weren't quite that Irish because my mother was a country recipient. Yeah. And my grandfather and grandmother were all people from Virginia or South Carolina who had moved to Mississippi about 1850.

Yeah, I just wondered, because sometimes those things are kept alive. Well, it's only been, I think, in 77 that my mother would sing Scottish songs to me, which she had learned, I think, from her aunt. It was like that. People, sometimes immigrants were a little ashamed of things and were suppressed. I guess that's true. And just never did talk about them very much. Maybe they had good reason. I never did get the members of the Melody Four down pat either. Speaking of being Irish down pat. That's an unconscious bond that came out.

Well, the Melody Four that I first played with in Marshall was composed of Jake Goldberg, a drummer, and Pye Atkins, James Atkins, excuse me, James Davis, Pye Davis, Piano, Tootie Buck ! Garrett, Clarinet, and me, saxophone. The first band I played with, for money, I played saxophone.
James Davis played what now?
Piano.
Oh, I've got it now.

I have pictures of that little group. We were, we made a movie in my hometown. And this time they had traveling producers who came around and put on hometown movies. And this one was called The Girl from Marshall. And we were the band. And in the movie I can remember very well a man calling for action and we were going through all the antics that the musicians did in those days. And we were going through the saxophone and the clarinet, you know, and jumping up on the piano.
Uh-huh.
Just, uh, it was, in fact we wore yama yama suits. We wore clown suits in the picture.
They were called yama yama?
Uh-huh.
Well, I know there was a song, Yama Yama Man, but I never knew what that meant.

I don't know, I don't, I really don't know the connection. But, uh, but suits with the pom poms like, uh, carnival suits that they used in the audience. Uh, they used to call them yama yama suits. I don't know why. I don't know.

Yeah, well I have to check on that. Well, certain things become fads like, Yeah. Uh, Rudolph Valentino's style. I know they used to have chic suits, I've heard of. Even a certain way they were cut and things. Must have been an invitation of the chic Rudolph Valentino.
They used to have jazz model suits too.
What was that?

Did you know that? Never. Well, that's something that I can tell you that is really cute, I think. In the twenties they had jazz model suits. And they were really jazzy too. Uh-huh. And they, uh, peg pants. Uh-huh. They had, uh, the pockets and the coats.
Uh-huh.

They were cut at extreme angles. Uh-huh. They had, uh, everything jazzy that you can think of and corny. It, uh, it was put into a suit and called a jazz model suit. They were advertised as jazz model suits. Uh-huh. And, uh, sold as such. I remember Blue Steel, who was a very famous orchestra leader. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. I saw him wearing one one time in, uh, in Shreveport, where I was located at the time. Some of the musicians wore these jazz model suits, but I can tell you that the Blue Melody Boys never did. We, we stuck to a little more conservative, uh, cut.
Which kind of boys?

The... The Buddy's Blue Melody Boys. Oh, the Melody Boys. Yeah, I see. This is a professional group that I played with later. Uh-huh. The Melody Four was just a little hometown group. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. At that time, uh, they had the Dixieland bands in neighborhoods just like we had rock bands a few years ago. Not, there weren't as many, but every town had three or four little bands that copied the, you know, original Dixieland jazz band.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. Well, uh, I'm getting a little out of order with my questions. Uh, we can jump around. And someday Johnny will edit this. When he, when he follows in my footsteps. We'll have him do all the dirty work. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh, where did, uh, Ham Crawford work, you say, in the, in all, that through the West?

Ham Crawford, uh, was a well-known name. And, uh, we talked about him before. Ham was a, a really fine saxophonist and, uh, played the clarinet. Played an E-flat clarinet, which he was a trickster with. He, uh, he's taught me how to break the clarinet in two and play on the upper, uh, section of the clarinet and juggle the other part and throw it on the legs. He was a real clown with a clarinet. Yes. This was, uh, part of the job in the twenties was, uh, getting over, selling, uh, herself in that respect. Ham was from Tyler, Texas. That's where I first knew him. He played with the original Jack Gardner Orchestra of Dallas, which was a prominent Dallas name in the twenties. And, uh, then he went out on his own and he was quite an experienced man. He was so, so much more experienced and, uh, knew the music business so much better than any of the younger kids. He always got young, ambitious kids who were ready to leave home and go play. And, uh, most of his playing really, when I played with him was North Louisiana. We established a music school in Shreveport. And he was also a teacher and a promoter. And he established this music school in Shreveport. He taught all the young society kids how to play saxophone and other instruments. And then we used this studio as a nightclub on Wednesdays and Saturday nights. They had booths and everything. It was a very popular place and only the nicest people came. But, Ham would, uh, have everything made. And then, boom, he decided he wanted to go off somewhere and he'd leave and leave good business and everything. But he just wanted to keep on the move a lot, you know. And, uh, uh, northeast Louisiana, all over Texas. He also played the oil fields of West Texas. I never was with him, but he was out in Ranger and Breckenridge, Cisco, all out through West Texas, uh, before coming to, uh, to our part of East Texas. And I joined him, uh, he had a trill that was extremely good and he got sick on this one occasion. And they had heard about me so they called Marshall and I met him in Palestine, Texas, and we played a job there that night. Piano and drums and clarinet. And so, just a little bit later, when Ham was reorganizing and adding to his band why he asked me to join. Of course, I just couldn't wait, you know. So, but later, and speaking of what he did, Ham would show up, uh, in Wichita, Kansas, for example. Uh, he would, uh, find out all, well, say, the best room. They were the best locally organized band. And he would take them over and take them on the road. Make big promises, which sometimes he kept. Sometimes it wasn't possible to keep them. But he, uh, he was important in my case because he started me out.
Uh-huh.
And, uh, I certainly learned a lot from him.
What kind of sax did he play?
What kind of sax do I play? No, did he play? Oh, Ham Crawford. Oh, Ham Crawford had a CG Conn, E flat alto.
Uh-huh.

He, the Conn factory had made him up a gold saxophone with rubies and diamonds and everything on the inside of the bell and on the outside. One of the fanciest things. Ted Lewis had one like it except Ted's cost a lot more money, I'm sure. But Conn made this up for Ham Crawford. And, uh, he used to put a light, had a little light hooked up with batteries and he would, uh, on waltzes he would go around the floor. Band would stay in the background. He would get out and mingle with all the people, uh, waltzing. And, uh, he'd have his light and his saxophone. It was quite a, quite a show. I'd never seen it done before. All of these things were new to, to me, because sure I wasn't a professional one. But Ham knew all of the tricks of the trade and, uh, I learned from him.
What about, uh, was Rudy Weidoff popular then?

Rudy Weidoff was extremely popular. Uh, he was a concert artist and, uh, a very popular Victor recording artist and, uh, is not given credit enough for the influence he had in popularizing the saxophone. Certainly he not only wrote for it, but he played it well and his records were sold by the thousands all over America. In fact, all over the world. Yeah.
Was he a showman like that or did you see him?

I doubt that. Boyd? I never did see him in person. Of Boyd's Center? I just copied his record. Boyd's Center I knew of real well, Boyd's Center and the Centipedes. Uh, in fact, I copied some, not copied, but I listened to his records and made an effort to copy some of them, which were on Paramount, I believe, at the time. And then he made Victor records with, uh, Jimmy and Tommy Dorsey and, uh, they were, they were called Boyd's Center and the Centipedes.

I just wondered if, if. They were good. I just wondered who else, and you mentioned Ted Lewis, and you keep thinking of different saxophones and clarinetes. Who, who had these tricks, supposedly, and, uh, at least certainly some of them technically did unusual things, novelty things.
Yeah, well, Jimmy, excuse me.
Yeah, go ahead.

Jimmy Maloney of Jimmy George, who played the two clarinets. Yeah. So beautifully together. Played them together and, and, and, real good. And I knew a guy in New Orleans who was with the, uh, Tom Guerin band who played three clarinets at one time.
Who was that?

His name was, uh, Jack Bunch. And he was with the band that Woody Herman started with in New Orleans at Club Forest in 1932. It was called Tom Guerinovich. Yeah. Later shortened to Tom Guerin. And his band, they were from San Francisco. Very popular in New Orleans. And, uh, anybody who played at Club Forest was popular, I'll tell you that. Ben Pollock played there. Yeah. And, uh, I visited Jack there. Snoozer Quinn, of course, was a big friend of mine. He was in New Orleans at the time. But, uh, tricks were all part of, uh, of the small bands of the day. Uh, in Mississippi, for example, they had a band called Watson's Bellhops. To this day, people over 60 years old frequently referred to the bellhops. Okay, Ezell and Raymond Watson were both saxophone players, brothers. And they organized this band. They dressed in bellhop uniforms. And, uh, they played everywhere. They played theaters and they played dances. And in Mississippi, they were most popular. In fact, Raymond finally ended up here in Jackson. Uh, his brother went on to New York and was always a very successful, uh, commercial, uh, musician. Recorded and made a lot of, a lot of records. But, Raymond died here. He, uh, never was very successful after he and his brother split up. But, he did have bands on up through the 30s, I believe. Right in Jackson.
Who did Ezell play with in New York?

Uh, I think the, uh, more possibly the Lanterns. Uh huh. And, uh, just jobbing all around town. I don't remember any big name bands. Uh, but he played with a lot of them, I'm sure. In fact, he's made some records. In, uh, recent years, uh, they're the type of music that was popular back in the 40s and 50s and even the 30s. But, I can't tell you who they, who the record were made with. But, it, in my mind, is somebody like the Lanterns, you know. Mm-hmm.
Something like, say, a gallimbardo type sound.
Uh.
Very sweet. Well.
Kind of sound. More like the Lantern sound, which is a fast tempo, uh, danceable type of music, uh, semi-arranged. Mm-hmm. Just good, good players.

Yeah. Always had good musicians. Uh, back to Hamm Crawford, we have mentioned some of the people with him. Uh huh. But, uh, could you name some of the people that were in the band when you were with him?

Yeah, I sure can, and some who were with him later who were remarkably good musicians. When I joined Hamm, he had a pianist named Eddie Whitley. He had, uh, a drummer named Buddy Seaman. And this Buddy Seaman was the Buddy of the Buddy's Blue Melody Boys, which was organized later, from a Hamm Crawford band. And he had a, uh, a guy named Harry Mullins on banjo. And a guy from St. Louis named George Shaw, who played trombone, banjo. He had an expert banjoist from Chicago named Connie Webster. And actually, Connie wasn't with this Crawford group I played with. He was with another group. But I believe that about covers the men in the band when I joined. And so, because we had two sax, trombone, they all doubled. At that time musicians, nearly every guy played two or three different instruments. And so, this was a good little band that we played all through southern Louisiana even, as well as north Louisiana. And I think I mentioned in our first interview that they were so different from the real jazz bands that they've had in southern Louisiana. They were a big hit. They wore white shirts and silk shirts and sashes. And, of course, this Hamm Crawford band was supposed to have been from Havana, Cuba. Always from Havana. He had played in Havana. So, that was one of his selling points. Had big banner back of the band, Hamm Crawford's Orchestra of Havana, Cuba. This was given to him by the Kahn Band Instrument Company. At that time it was popular for the band instrument companies to make up felt background signs. Kahn was most promotional minded. And any band with a fairly good name could get these from Kahn free of charge. They'd make them up specially for them.

I know somebody who still makes. Is that right? She occasionally does it for, you know, a social organization. She makes them for the New Leviathan Oriental Foxtrot Orchestra. I don't know if you've heard them or not. I've told you about them.
Well, I remember this. That's Leviathan Orchestra back in the, oh, God knows when, 1920s.

Well, this is a band that plays stocks. Uh-huh. Oh, yeah. Yeah, I told you about them. Yes. And they try to bring back every detail directly. Which is nice that they're doing that. And it's marvelous to see things done that way. Anyway, uh, you told me about some band that you went to Lake Charles with.

Well, this was part of the Ham Crawford band because we changed personnel. And this was Brooks Pruitt and Dick Coleman and Buddy Seaton and myself and a boy from Software, Louisiana, named Alvin Tonietta, who was a local guy who played trumpet. But now, I was going to tell you about some men who played with Ham Crawford earlier, I mean later. Dick, he went to San Antonio and did the usual thing of reorganizing a band to take out on the road and it was easy to get guys to go. Among these people that he is was Gilbert O'Shaughnessy.
Oh, yeah.

And Gilbert is one of my favorite clarinet players, always. I was crazy about him. I learned a lot from him just listening to him play with Ham because he was outstanding. He later played with Jimmy Joyce, made all the recordings with Jimmy. He didn't play many courses but he was the clarinet, the best clarinetist in Texas in my opinion.
Yeah. In fact, he sort of reminded me of rap if I remember correctly. That's possible.
I can remember. Well, it's been years since I've listened to those records.
I don't have time to listen to records anymore.
That's right.
You know, you work.
Yeah.
As I say, I've been triple dipping lately.

But he had Bill Francisco on drums and again George Shaw on trombone and Connie Webster on banjo and always a good group of musicians. He was a commercial good saxophone player. And, but he could always track these good men. And, you have to start somewhere. And I'm very thankful that I started with him. Well, the fact that he knew the trade. And, I learned a lot from him.
Well, these people in Lake Chaucer, did they have a name?

Ham Crawford Orchestra No. 2 is the number that, is the name we went under there because we were still supposed to be working for Ham. We played Shell Beach, Pleasure Pier. We played Big Lake out from Lake Charles. We played, we played Jennings, all the little towns surrounding Lake Charles. And it was just a four piece outfit with Alvin Torniette who we used when we could on trumpet. And so we had five pieces really. And then, I think I mentioned that they had little black bands who played ballyhood for, they had a little ship, a little pleasure boat that would take you from Lake Charles out to Big Lake. And these little black bands, ballyhood, before they, people would come on the boat. But we'd go out and play for the big dancers. In fact, they had this big ballroom out there, Dick, that had a big crystal ball like you'd think you'd find in Chicago. That was just a country ballroom right on Big Lake.
Did you know Nellie Lutcher on Lake Charles?
Lutcher?
Nellie Lutcher. She's a piano player. She later recorded for Capitol.
That name is very familiar.

That's one of those family bands. I forget what they called it. I think they were an Imperial Band or something like that. And Paul Barnes was playing around there. Pullo Barnes, you know, you'd have one of those French nicknames, even if his last name was Barnes. He was from New Orleans, I remember playing, but mainly alto. I remember one of those fast-fingering alto players that you used to get then. And I guess they'd get them in the first.
Carl Borsick was pretty fast.
Yeah. There were a lot of them. Well, of course, you hear Weedhoff and Jimmy Dorsey, even. I mean, that kind of fingering. And Al Galladero, it tripped his hat to Weedhoff.
Most certainly. He played all of those things. In fact, Galladero was really a great saxophonist and playing there's no question about it. And bassoon player. I didn't know he played bassoon.
I think he played bassoon for Toscanini. He must have been fair, at least. Yeah.
But his career was interesting because he left New Orleans and went on up. Last time I saw him, I was playing with Paul Wyman's big band.
Well, he's...
And he was with him for a number of years.
He's still around New York the last time I...
I would imagine. Is Tony Prentice still living?

No, he is not. He's passed on. I hadn't talked to his wit or anything. I never did really know her. Now, that's a fellow who did something that most people don't realize. If you had to choose one musician in this country who really started the ball rolling right time, I'd say it was Tony Prentice. Because he got a couple of writers in New York interested in it. And he would record them with his band and his trio. And from that, they wrote a book. And you never know what will happen out of an idea of something like that.
Right. Well, I just... I think Tony recorded with John Detroit, didn't he?

Not that I know him. I forget the name of the clarinet player. I'd know it if you said it in a minute. But he was with Johnny before the recordings, if I remember correctly. And I don't know why I can't think of the guy's name. But he's one of those forgotten clarinet players who played very, very well. It seemed to me Johnny Harmon liked his playing. I was surprised when the records came out, how good the man played. A lot of times you forget about people.
Oh, it's true.
You can't. You can't remember everybody.
And particularly in New Orleans, of course, there were just so many of them.
Yeah, clarinet.

And always of the instruments that I think the new audience playing, I think the clarinetist and of course trumpet, trombone, except for good tailgate and good playing, well, of course, Charlie Miller and Julian Lane played well and there were others. But there never was a tromboneist example like Jack or, of course, there weren't many of those ever. But today, of course, the style that he created is used by everybody to some extent. But just somehow, to me, except for Brunus and Santo and the others, who played well, beautiful. But they were not, they didn't create any particular style, Dick, I don't think. Well, tailgate was something that they perfected to some extent. They, they, the blacks have done it always. But, the clarinet and trumpet are distinctive instruments. I don't think saxophone even, but the way the saxophone players were at all comparable to the, to the clarinetists. They just always had wonderful clarinet players and the black players, you know, like Bonnie and so many others, who were one of my favorites of all time.
And, if you had to name a single famous New Orleans saxophone player, you could name one, I'd say. Eddie Miller, of course.

Eddie, Eddie is an original. Yeah. In a sense, he, he certainly created a style of his own. His playing is distinctive. He's an extremely talented man. And probably, if you wanted to hear his clarinet playing, I don't know, Leon Rapolo's playing real well. But, it's my feeling probably that Eddie would probably play more like him than anybody. If you listen to some of the quirky courses that he made that would have even credited to him, they would amaze you. Have you heard the Bud Brown record with Eddie? Oh, yeah.
I got that. I guess Bud gave it to me on, either him or the guitar player. I mean, you know.
Eddie, Eddie does play some clarinet on there.

Not the guitar player. The guy who wrote one of the pieces on there. He's a guitarist. Yeah. Eddie, of course, he disclaims being in shape on clarinet. And I heard him record with Johnny Armand on clarinet. Oh, he? He said he hadn't played it for nine years or something like that.
Yeah.
What difference did he make when he played? But, it is a funny thing about trombone, because how many bands had trombones when you were there?

Well, of course, I was there doing a depressed era. And there were very few trombones being used, except in the big spot job in bands. They always used trombone in full sections, but the little joints, they just dropped trombone. That's it. They used trumpet, clarinet, dubbing sax, and bass, drums, and piano. For example, Freddie Newman's band at the Silver Slipper consisted of Sharky. Actually it was Sharky's band at that time. Freddie Newman was playing piano, Ching Martin was playing bass, Mark Hazel was playing drums, Nina Pecone was playing tenor and clarinet. And that was a good little band, but no trombone. So, they just didn't, there was that period of time when they didn't use them. Now, I'm speaking of white bands.
Yeah.

Almost always I speak, in my conversation, as many wonderful black bands as there were in the Warriors, the time I was there, I just got to hear them on parades and got to hear them valley hunting for various fairs on a wagon or truck.
You might know them in the store or something.
Oh, I knew. They would come into Whirland. I got to meet a lot of them in the store, I sure did. And among them, of course, Paul Burberon and A.J. Perron. Very many, many others. Right.
So many musicians down there, but the impression of the trombone is especially interesting to me. I think of somebody like, I wonder what happened to Ellis Stratkos during that period. Where was he?
Well, after I met Ellis when he had just come in for a tour with Norman Brownlee's band. And I guess there wasn't much work around there because it was right in the middle of
the Depression.

And the next thing I heard of him, he was secretary of the union in Biloxi and running a candy shop. That's the last I've heard of Ellis, but I knew him real well. He was a gentleman and extremely nice man.
And where was he from?
I guess Biloxi. Because that's where he went back to and I think probably his father had been in the candy business. And he took it over.
What's the getting about Big... Big Spider-Man?
No, Pruitt.
Oh, Brooks Pruitt.
Brooks Pruitt and Dick Coleman.
I'm coming out with Brooks and Dick and getting Bigs. Yeah. But who were they?

Well, now, Brooks Pruitt was a really wonderful pianist. And Brooks was from Laurel, Mississippi instead. But he came over into Arkansas when I first met him. And he played outstanding piano. He played with the Buddies Blue Melody Boys. He was the pianist in the group that we used in Lake Charles. And he was an original pianist with the Buddies Blue Melody Boys. It was a band that I played with for about three years. And Pruitt wasn't always the pianist. He was the first pianist. But he was a very interesting character. Back then he liked to travel and he would leave us and go out to California. Finally ended up in Dallas, played with all the best Dallas bands. And he played with Blue Steel. Not when Blue Steel was a recording orchestra, but at other times. He was a very famous character. Blue Steel was. And you could write a book about Blue Steel. I'd rather not. But I'd rather you wouldn't either, because there'd be too many bad things to tell. I don't want everybody to tell.
No, they say he was a real character. Yeah.

He always, he was crazy about me though, as far as, our paths were always, they crossed pleasantly. For example, in the oil fields, there were always people trying to give you trouble. And Steel was a very big six-footer and tough as a boot. He used to come around and say, look boy, if they give you any trouble, just tell me. Just tell me. Yeah. I'll get them.
He might, he might reach for something. Yeah.
Take care of him.
He was really tough, I'd be.

Well, he was. He was an organizer and he was in the Navy. He was a prize fighter and he was just generally as tough. And that's one of the things we used to have an exciting time on our band when Blue Steel and Brooks Pruitt, who was another six-footer and tough.
Mm-hmm.
We, we just kept holding our breaths and, of course, we were afraid at any time we were going to break into a big battle between those two. Never did happen. What happened to Brooks Pruitt?
Is he still alive?
Well, Brooks died in Fort Worth, Texas. Meaning he's been dead about 20 years or at least 20, 25 years.
Did I ask you about the Western Swing or I would prefer to call it Western Jazz Band around Fort Worth and Dallas? Did you ever hear any of those?

Uh, during my playing years, they didn't exist as far as I knew. Mm-hmm. Speaking of in the 20s. Mm-hmm. Uh, country and Western bands and even hillbilly bands were practically, uh, unknowable. There, there may have been some, but I, I didn't know them. Uh.
You didn't know about Light Crush Pruitt and all that stuff. Uh. Light Crush Doe Boys, I mean. The Light Crush Doe Boys?

Oh, uh, that was considerably later. Later that you learned about that. Let's see, I'm speaking even when radio was very young and, uh, there were no, uh, that I can remember, there were no string bands, really, what we called them.
Mm-hmm.

Uh, at that time, the, uh, Bob Wills and all of those, uh, bands came a little later. Yeah. But, uh, Dixieland bands were popular in Texas. And, uh, the, uh, of course the college orchestras like Jimmy Joy's and Shakey's and various other Texas Jazzers from Austin College. Mm-hmm. They were all about routine, uh, small clarinet, trumpet, trombone, drums and piano bands. Mm-hmm. And, uh, there could have been the other country bands, but, uh, I, I just really did not, didn't run into them. Yeah. They came from, I guess, about 1926 on, until now. But I watched the development of them, been very interested in them. I know a lot about country musicians and country bands.
Yeah, Pud played with the, Pud Brown played with the Rice Brothers, he said, and I thought they'd run it.
Well, Pud played with Phil Levant, too, I don't know if you ever heard that. No, I don't know. Extremely popular name band, back in the 30s and 40s. But, Pud's an experienced hand.

He's played with everybody. Yeah, well, there were a lot of, Benny Strickler was a good one who played, like there were those country and western bands and the jazz musician Obscure. Yeah. We talked about so many people. I don't know who the Texas jazzers are. Well, that's a, that's a...

It was a small band from Austin College in Texas. They were very popular. Charles Robert Ballou was a pianist, and Smith Ballou, who was a famous orchestra leader and movie star and banjo player, was a member of it. D. Or, who later went to St. Louis and played with all the St. Louis big bands. And Jack Brown, the trombones, who was a very good trombone player. And what did D. Or play?
Charlie Potts.

D. Or was a drummer. He followed music and went on to play with pretty big time bands in St. Louis and around. And Charlie Potts, who was a saxophonist and clarinetist. He was, he was good. He was a member of a family who had a big jewelry business. So when the time came for him to go into business, he just had to leave the saxophone alone. But I think those, there were several of those fellows who really were ace musicians.
Would you be listening to black bands like Alfonso Trent, Troy Floyd, Don Albert?

Very much so. Don Albert? Don Albert, I hadn't heard at that time. I did hear him in 1930 in Vermont, and he was great. But Alfonso Trent, I have written a lot about Alfonso, I mean to different people like Frank Dricks and so on. Because I heard him at the Adolphus Hotel in Dallas, at which time this was the fanciest and best hotel in Texas. And they were good. They just were good. And they were, I mean this was before Basie and before any of those bands, even the Kansas City bands like George Lee and Benny Moulton and Basie and all the rest of them, Jay McShann. But this was a, it was a kind of a, the type of band that some of the black musicians of New Orleans who had society bands, really. And they were good. They played jazz, they played whatever. Because they held down a wonderful job and had a good sound, as I remember.
Well behaved, well dressed?

Yeah. Always. In fact, it's, I've always remarked that among the organized black bands, there was always great deal of pride in playing. And they were respected. And they almost always made an extreme effort to look the part. Always. I can say that of any of the black bands that I ever saw. I'm, I'm barring country blues players and others who. You mean the big bands, you're talking about the name bands. I'm speaking of territorial bands, organized black bands. They were very good. And they, that's the only thing they did. I mean, they, they were professional. And they might have starved some, like white bands did too. But they always had a, the idea of having a really good band.

And Tom told me, Don Albert once told me that he'd be out on the road. And times would be hard. And I would be eating cheese and crackers. And he would pull up Bob Crosby's band bus. And they'd just need it. And all, that was the way you lived. You ate cheese and crackers and shared, shared alike. That's an unbelievable period.
Well, I can tell you, and I may be repeating myself for my former interview, but, uh, Jasper Tompkins, who was our agent.
Mm-hm.

And, uh, Shreveport, and who booked as many black bands as he did white. Uh, used to tell me, Shucks, said, Tim, y'all are too persnickety. I get black bands, if we have a bad night, I just go get a couple loads of bread and a lot of bologna, and man, they go right to it. And they're satisfied. So, that bears out what you said. Yeah. But that was, uh, everybody panicked in those years. The dance band business was always very difficult after 1929. It was good from 1922 until about 1929. But, uh, those years from 19, late 29 up through 1933, when it started coming back, 34, it was a rough business for even big name bands, though, they were still.

But still, people would pay to go hear a 10 or 12 piece band, and you had no problem getting the musicians willing to go on the road and rehearse, and do all of the things that were required to have, oh, 14 piece bands in the thirties. Oh, yeah. Now, that doesn't make economic sense.

Well, a lot of bands would, uh, during a period of organization, for example, they would, the leader would make an arrangement with a hotel. And, uh, the hotel would say, give them room and board. They would play luncheon and dinner. And, uh, then maybe they'd book out nights to make cash money until the band was organized. And, uh, it's really true that, uh, that leaders would get a hold of a little money, and they would generally, uh, let the guys draw a dollar a day. Uh-huh. And, uh, if they were able to get that room and board deal, pretty soon they'd be off of the money. But that's, that was the truth.

Can you name a hotel that was built in this country during the Depression? No. I mean, I don't think there was one. I read a book on hotels once. Uh-huh. And just by coincidence, and it comes to mind, that maybe the things were hard for the hotels, too, and they could afford to put up bands very cheaply, because they weren't going to sell those rooms anyway.
Well, that's very true.
Yeah.

Um, I had a band in 1930 that was a real good little band, seven piece band, and we stayed at the Hotel Edson in Beaumont, Texas. Uh-huh. Two dollars and seventy-five cents each per week. And we played every Saturday night on the roof. Uh-huh. And that was the only guarantee that we had. The rest of the time we booked out all of them through that.
Uh-huh.
Good country, but poor country around southern Louisiana.
Uh-huh.
And I told you that, though, when I rambled on that first time that we talked. But it's the maximum. Two dollars and seventy-five cents each. A week.
Did you get paid for playing on Saturday night?
Oh, on Saturday nights, yes, that was a ten-dollar job. We'd make it on through the whole week. If we didn't book another job, we'd still have that ten bucks.
Oh, weren't you?
We had a seventy-span. We got seventy dollars.
Uh-huh.
That was cash. And we paid our rent, of course, out of that. Two seventy-five.
And you weren't getting double for Lita?
No, I wasn't getting double for Lita. And I was setting up music stands and everything else, too. But there was so little money that we're glad to.
Because I think Lita's ought to get triple.
I do, too. I mean, I'm serious.
I do, too. It is an unbearable job, when you think of what they have to put up with.
Right. But it was very common for bands to expect a Lita to do all the work and book the dates. And then have what was called a commonwealth band and it was split right down. Everybody got the same.

Think of how many phone calls a Lita would have to make, how many telegrams he'd have to send. And the expenses must have just been, well, of course it was cheap then, but it was a terrible thing for a Lita to have to do out of making ten dollars on a job.

Yeah. But you must remember that the money was so very scarce. And I played many jobs throughout East Texas and southern Louisiana where we'd be playing for an American Legion dance or an Elf's Club or something like that where we didn't have a guarantee that it would be a subscription dance and sometimes we'd make three bucks, sometimes we'd make seven bucks, sometimes we didn't make anything. Of course they were generally booked on a seven to thirty basis. And so, to kind of get back to New Orleans, I remember an agent in New Orleans named Frank that, uh, that, uh, Fake memory of something like that. But anyway, he booked all the little bands out into the territory. And, uh, the, uh, a lot of, he just used a lot of New Orleans musicians. I think Dutch was playing a lot with Frank when I first met him. Dutch Andrews, uh. Mm-hmm. And, uh, Burton. But he was just, anybody he could get, he would book dates and he'd organize the bands and strictly non-union. Mm-hmm. But, uh, I just wondered if you had ever heard of him.

I don't recall the name really, but I probably have heard it because it sounds vaguely familiar. Yeah, I suspect he's long since dead. Well, I've heard too many names anyway. Yeah. Well, that's right. Yeah, you, you know, people like you and I were constantly working with names. You just can't remember everybody. Right. And, uh, anyway, uh, I hate to keep coming back to the same people, but we never did get to Dick Coleman. Excuse me.
Well, that's not your fault.
This is good stuff. Yeah. I'm just trying to follow up. That's what I keep a list of questions here for. Yeah.

Dick Coleman was, uh, a banjo player. Wow. And a vocalist, and he was very good. He was, uh, he went to the University of Alabama. He was a Kappa Alpha. And extremely popular with the ladies. Uh-huh. And, uh, so he was, uh, one of the original members of the Brothers Brumelty Boys, also. See, this thing went through so many changes. I, uh, the original Brothers Brumelty Boys, uh, Pruitt and Dick Coleman were both in that band. Uh-huh. And, uh, Dick, uh, he was with a lot of different bands. And, uh, he and Pruitt were big buddies. They were big drinking buddies, and they were always having the time. At that time, the rest of us were young. We didn't care and think much about drinking at all. But Pruitt and Dick made up for it. And, uh, so when our bands finally broke up, Dick went on back to Sheffield, Alabama, where his home was. And I don't know what happened to him after that. But, uh, most of the men I played with, I'll say a lot of them I have kept up with through the years. But, uh, never did know what happened to Dick. The next group of Buddy Brumelty Boys, see, we changed. We got entirely, uh, new fellas. And, uh, in the next group that was together for two and a half years without, almost without a break, we had, uh, Rhodes Cook on piano. We had, uh, Bobby Turley, who was well known on drums. He played with a lot of big, clean bands. And, uh, Red Roundtree, who was later to be a staff guitarist with, uh, the movie studios in California, who's still living in, who I visited. And, uh, Shockey Wilcox, who we mentioned in that other interview I believe. And, uh, Footscad on trombone. And me on clarinet. Well we played pretty good music. And, uh, for about two and a half years we were organized and traveled all over east and north Texas and Arkansas and played everywhere. We, we really had, uh, I think that was probably my most enjoyable, uh, playing that I did as far as, uh, playing that was concerned. And I finally, after Buddy Brumelty Boys broke up, I went with the Louisiana Rambles, who we had talked about and who I think really had the best band that I ever heard in those times. They, uh, I was not with them when they were at their best, in my opinion. But they had arrangements, they had a big band, and it was just absolutely remarkable. It was better than anything that I'd ever heard in New Orleans or anywhere. And, uh, and unfortunately they never recorded. But they had three South Lizziganians with them, the Pat and Bob Dequeer, the East Brothers, and Rome Landry, who's still an active drummer in Houston, Texas. But we talked a lot about them, and I tell you, they were extremely good. And I joined them, and we still had a fabulous band, but the first band they had, uh, consisted of this Burt Sigerson, who we talked about on saxophone, Bob Cole on saxophone. Don Ellis, who was an extremely good saxophonist, and, uh, Pat and Bob, and, uh, the leader was a man named Bob Canfield, who was an extremely good arranger and who worked with these boys. They had Paul Brown on bass, who Johnny Hyman played with, uh, later. You know, most of my knowledge of this subject is, uh, based on Texas, Louisiana, not as much as in New Orleans as, uh, as it is outside of New Orleans. But I've tried to kind of keep this, uh, in New Orleans and Louisiana, everybody. If you'd like to, if you'd like to tell you anything about many other bands that I'd be talking to.
Well, uh, we won't, maybe we can do another reel, huh? Uh-huh. And talk, talk about Mississippi musicians. Of course, I want to talk about a lot of people. I don't know where Bert Sigerson is now.
Yeah, right, right.

To find him, you've reminded me of that, you know. Uh, what Sidney Ayrton used to call a BAME system clarinet, what he called an Alba system. Yeah. What did you say it was? Well, Sidney referred to the Alba system clarinet as a Fuki.
He referred to the BAME system clarinet as a Fuki. D-F bamboo

Well, this is Tim Kelly again, the second reel. And we got to talking about Kelly and how the great musicians were attracted, you were saying. And I never didn't know anything about Max Fink, at least I didn't remember. Well, he was

before your time. He was a violinist and a very extremely popular character in New Orleans history. Played in the theaters and played for all the carnival balls and things like that. Well, Ted Frank, yes. I loved Ted Frank and I knew his father before him. And Dave who established the sheet meat business at Welland.

segments.title: Opening: names and setting at the Archives and History building
segments.summary: Allen and Kelly give their names; Jones is introduced and the purpose, a follow-up interview partly to train Jones, is explained.

segments.title: World War I, the war bond drive and Kelly's sisters
segments.summary: Kelly worked war bond drives with the Boy Scouts around age 12, just before taking up clarinet; his two sisters studied piano.

segments.title: Armistice Day 1918 in Marshall, Texas
segments.summary: Kelly recalls the town's Armistice celebration and the local Baptist college's ROTC.

segments.title: Leaving Marshall to join Ham Crawford's band
segments.summary: Kelly left high school around 1922 to go out with the Ham Crawford band and has worked as a musician since.

segments.title: Ham Crawford's travels, and first hearing of Wingy and the Crescent City Jazzers
segments.summary: Crawford recruited the best young local players; Kelly first heard of Wingy from a New Orleans band photo and recalls the Riddick brothers.

segments.title: Allen asks about Mobile players in that band
segments.summary: Allen names Avery Loposa and Felix Carino; Kelly did not know them.

segments.title: Kelly's Irish family background and lack of musical ancestry
segments.summary: Kelly says the family was theatrical and well educated but not musical; his grandparents came from Virginia and South Carolina to Mississippi around 1850.

segments.title: The Melody Four, The Girl from Marshall movie and yama yama suits
segments.summary: Kelly's first paid band, the Melody Four, played in a hometown movie wearing yama yama clown suits.

segments.title: Jazz model suits and neighborhood Dixieland bands
segments.summary: Kelly describes 1920s jazz model suits, Blue Steel wearing one, and every town having small Dixieland bands.

segments.title: Ham Crawford as a trickster, teacher and promoter
segments.summary: Crawford, from Tyler, played the E-flat clarinet with tricks, ran a music school and nightclub in Shreveport, and took bands on the road; Kelly joined him in Palestine, Texas.

segments.title: Ham Crawford's jeweled Conn saxophone
segments.summary: Conn made Crawford a gold saxophone with rubies and a light, which he played while waltzing around the floor.

segments.title: Rudy Wiedoeft and Boyd Senter as saxophone and clarinet influences
segments.summary: Kelly praises Wiedoeft's popularizing of saxophone and says he copied Boyd Senter's records.

segments.title: Novelty clarinetists, Tom Gerun's band and Watson's Bellhops
segments.summary: Kelly recalls double and triple clarinet players, Club Forest in New Orleans in 1932, and Mississippi's Watson's Bellhops brothers.

segments.title: Personnel of the Ham Crawford band and its Havana backdrop
segments.summary: Kelly names the men in Crawford's band when he joined and describes the Orchestra of Havana, Cuba banner supplied by Conn.

segments.title: Later Crawford alumni, including clarinetist Gilbert O'Shaughnessy
segments.summary: Crawford reorganized in San Antonio with players such as Gilbert O'Shaughnessy, whom Kelly admired; Kelly says he learned a lot from Crawford.

segments.title: Ham Crawford Orchestra No. 2 around Lake Charles
segments.summary: Kelly's small group played Lake Charles resorts and Big Lake under the Crawford name, with black bands advertising from the boat.

segments.title: Lake Charles musicians, fast alto players and Al Gallodoro
segments.summary: Allen asks about Nellie Lutcher and Paul Barnes; talk turns to fast-fingering alto players and Al Gallodoro's career.

segments.title: Tony Parenti and forgotten New Orleans clarinetists
segments.summary: Allen credits Tony Parenti with helping start the revival; both note how many clarinetists New Orleans had.

segments.title: New Orleans clarinet, trombone and saxophone styles; Eddie Miller
segments.summary: Kelly says clarinet and trumpet were New Orleans' distinctive instruments and calls Eddie Miller an original stylist.

segments.title: Trombones in Depression-era New Orleans bands and the Silver Slipper
segments.summary: Small white bands dropped trombone, as at Sharkey's Silver Slipper band; Kelly met black bandsmen in the Werlein's store.

segments.title: Ellis Stratkos, trombonist turned Biloxi union secretary
segments.summary: Kelly met Stratkos on a tour with Norman Brownlee's band in the Depression; he later ran a candy shop in Biloxi.

segments.title: Brooks Pruitt and Blue Steel
segments.summary: Kelly describes pianist Brooks Pruitt of Buddy's Blue Melody Boys and the tough bandleader Blue Steel, who looked out for Kelly in the oil fields.

segments.title: Western swing, the Light Crust Doughboys and Texas college bands
segments.summary: Kelly says country bands were unknown in his early years; he describes the Texas Jazzers from Austin College and their members.

segments.title: Black territory bands: Alfonso Trent and Don Albert
segments.summary: Kelly heard Alfonso Trent at the Adolphus in Dallas and remarks on the pride and professionalism of black territorial bands.

segments.title: Hard times in the dance band business after 1929
segments.summary: Kelly recalls agent Jasper Tompkins and how leaders used hotel room-and-board deals during the Depression.

segments.title: Pay at the Hotel Edson in Beaumont, commonwealth bands and a New Orleans agent
segments.summary: Kelly's 1930 seven-piece band got room for $2.75 a week and ten dollars for Saturday night; the leader's workload and a New Orleans booking agent are discussed.

segments.title: Dick Coleman, the later Blue Melody Boys and the Louisiana Rambles
segments.summary: Kelly describes banjoist Dick Coleman, the second Blue Melody Boys lineup that toured Texas and Arkansas, and the Louisiana Rambles band he joined afterward.

segments.title: End of reel one: clarinet system talk
segments.summary: Allen proposes another reel on Mississippi musicians and recalls Sidney Arodin's name for a clarinet system; the tape degenerates into repeated noise.

segments.title: Reel two begins: Max Fink and New Orleans violinists
segments.summary: Allen resumes on the second reel and asks about Max Fink; Kelly describes him as a violinist in New Orleans theaters and carnival balls, and mentions Ted Frank.
